1uxj9hp:278: Hermes introduces regex-based threat pattern recognition at the Memory write layer—a pragmatic but limited security measure. Pragmatic because: it blocks the most common prompt injection patterns at extremely low computational cost, without needing complex NLP models for semantic analysis. Limited because: regex cannot defend against semantic-level injection attacks (such as bypassing pattern matching through natural language descriptions). This suggests: for self-improving systems, prompt injection defense requires multi-layer strategies—an input layer (regex/rule filtering), a reasoning layer (having the model judge content reasonableness before writing), and an audit layer (post-hoc inspection of recorded content). Most agent frameworks today only implement the first layer, which is insufficient in high-adversarial scenarios.
1v95gpm:306: Hermes chooses to design dedicated tools for the skill mechanism (skill_list/skill_view/skill_manage) rather than using generic read/write tools to operate skill files—a design decision with deep engineering-philosophy considerations. Generic tools offer higher flexibility (one tool can do everything) but increase the cognitive burden and error rate of model invocation; dedicated tools offer lower flexibility but make the model's tool selection clearer and less error-prone. This reflects a core tension in agent system design: how to balance "tool specialization" and "tool uniformity." Hermes's answer: for high-frequency, standardized operations (like skill management), dedicated tools outperform generic ones; for low-frequency, innovative operations (like arbitrary file editing), generic tools are more appropriate.

1yhb5iq:330: Hermes' self-improving system consists of three complementary mechanisms, each layer targeting a different type of knowledge: the Memory layer stores stable factual information (user preferences, environment configuration), characterized by automatic injection at session startup — the Agent can sense it without actively calling; the Skill layer stores procedural knowledge (operation steps, best practices), requiring the Agent to actively call skill_view to load it, and proactively patch it when problems are found during use; the Session Search layer stores the complete thinking trajectory of trial and error, retrieved on demand, and activated only when the user mentions past conversations. The brilliance of this three-layer design is that each layer's persistence strategy and invocation frequency are highly matched with the update frequency and cognitive value of that layer's knowledge. Highly stable information (such as user preferences) suits low-frequency persistent storage; information that needs frequent trial-and-error accumulation (such as bug-fixing processes) suits on-demand retrieval rather than staying resident in context.

53qvbk:1660: ] In the following cases, the Agent proactively saves memory: user correction — “remember this” / “don't do that again”; user preferences — name, role, timezone, coding style, communication habits; environment discovery — OS, installed tools, project structure, API versions; convention learning — project-specific norms, tool quirks, workflows; stable facts — information still useful in future sessions. Session Search: learning from raw conversations. Memory stores conclusions, Skill stores methods, but real learning often happens during trial and error: failed attempts, wrong assumptions, sudden insights don't automatically become Memory or Skill, yet they contain valuable experience. Suppose the user asks: “How did we fix that bug last time?” Memory might remember “user uses Python 3.9”; Skill might remember “general bug-fixing procedure”. But the exact line of code that solved the problem, the key error message, the order of the trial-and-error — these exist only in the raw conversation. The specific session search technical solution is as follows: • FTS5 full-text indexing: all messages are indexed in real time into SQLite's FTS5 virtual table; • relevance ranking: sorted by keyword match score; • session grouping: take the most relevant few sessions; • LLM summary: use a cheap model (e.g., Gemini Flash) to generate a summary with metadata; • return result: not the full raw conversation, but an LLM-generated summary containing the complete narrative thread of “problem → attempted process → final solution”. Memory, skills, and session all store past experience. Memory is “passive recall” — automatically loaded each session, the Agent knows it without actively calling a tool; Skill is “active loading + self-maintenance” — the Agent needs to call skill_view to read details, and can use skill_manage to create new skills or repair outdated ones; Session Search is “on-demand recall” — it only searches when the user mentions past conversations, and does not stay resident in context. The comparison among the three is shown in the table below: mechanism | storage content | usage | role in Self-Improving. Memory: stable facts (user preferences, environment information); automatically injected into System Prompt each session; proactively added/modified via the memory tool; avoids re-asking already-confirmed information. Skill: procedural knowledge (operation steps, best practices); index (name + description) shown in System Prompt, full content loaded on demand via skill_view; created/modified/deleted via skill_manage; avoids re-inventing validated processes. Session Search: raw conversation history (complete thinking trajectory); proactively searches keywords via the session_search tool, LLM generates a structured summary; avoids stepping into already-encountered pitfalls. A complete self-improve workflow is as follows, achieving a higher starting point for the next task than the previous one: • Step 1: user asks “help me summarize this week's HN front page headlines and send them to Telegram”; • Step 2: Agent starts a session, the system prompt automatically contains: USER.md (“User prefers short summaries”) and the Skills index (discovers the “weekly-digest” skill is relevant); • Step 3: Agent calls skill_view("weekly-digest") to load the skill and executes step by step; • Step 4: during execution, discovers the skill's “RSS scraping” is outdated — the user actually uses the HN API. Agent calls skill_manage(action='patch') to update the skill; • Step 5: user says “only 5 headlines from now on”. Agent calls memory(action='add', target='user', content='User wants HN digest capped at 5 headlines'); • Step 6: disk updates, but the current session's system prompt does not change; • Step 7: next week the user asks the same question again. At startup, the system prompt already contains the new memory and the patched skill. The user does not need to repeat “only 5” or correct the skill's error.
